Neoliberal institutionalists focus more on the roles of International Institutions in their effectiveness in guarding peace amongst liberal societies. They believe that because International Institutions reduce uncertainty, and because uncertainty increases the probability of conflict, the reduction causes by International Institutions is more effective therefore at keeping the peace.
International Institutions also reduce transactions costs. So during crisis negotiations because two states have experience negotiating through the international institutions negotiations tend to go smoother. International Institutions can also hold states accountable by providing punitive restrictions. International Institutions can also provide dispute resolution, for example arbitration through the WTO for countries that have trade conflict.




Slightly different version of Liberal Peace. When countries have financial independence they tend to remain peaceful with eachother.
The more trade between states the more peaceful those states tend to be with eachother.
Tying Hands and Sunk Cost mechanism:
If you tie your hands and make your threat credible. If I have spent too much money (sunk cost) and my hands are tied my threat is much more credible.
When a country is much more dependent on one country then when the less dependent country makes a threat it can be viewed as credible. This will lead to a higher probability of a negotiated peace or policy change.
However, the empirical finding of this situation is mixed.



Trade reduces conflict is the hypothesus, however, there is not an empirical finding that clearly backs that idea.
First, how do you measure trade dependence? - Weak Link Measure: Between State 1 and State 2, given the total trade volume between the two states divided by GDP for both countries:
$$
\frac{\text{Total Trade Volume}}{\text{GDP}_1} \lt \frac{\text{Total Trade Volume}}{\text{GDP}_2}
$$

Therefore, State 1 is the weak link because less of it's GDP comes with the trade from State 1. While State 1 may have more resources to fight, it can avoid conflict by just trading which makes it less likely to initiate conflict. 

Salience Symmetry: When neither state is particularly dependent or both are equally dependent conflict is less likely overall.
Endogeneity: Since we cannot clearly say that trade prevents or causes conflict and vice versa, Endogenity argues that with a high probability of conflict trade will reduce. Because both trade and coflict have a negative correlation with eachother, reduced trade as a result of conlfict is a side effect of conflict not a cause of it.

What instruments are good predictors of trade? These are Endogenous factors, they do not cause or are not caused by conflict but because of these factors the level of trade is predicted. So therefore, trade doesn’t predict war but the endogenous (indepdent factors) that affect trade are said to be the cause or prevention of conflict.
Endogoeous means from within, so factors from within a country that affect it’s willingness to trade with another country or have a conflict.

Trade doens’t necessarily prevent war

So by this logic there is correlation between trade and peace is just as strong between trade and conflict.

text:
We make 4 key assumptions:

States are rational actors
States are modeled as unitary actors
We assume the issue is always somewhat divisible
Each side has complete info

We assume that any agreement inside the bargaining range is more beneficial to both sides than an outcome achieved through war.
Let the disputed good be normalized to 1. A wins the war with probability \(P_A\), and B wins with probability \(P_B = 1 - P_A\).
Fighting costs each side something, \(C_A > 0\) and \(C_B > 0\). These costs are paid whether the side wins or loses.
Each side’s expected payoff from war is therefore
\[W_A = P_A(1) + (1 - P_A)(0) - C_A = P_A - C_A\] \[W_B = P_B(1) + (1 - P_B)(0) - C_B = 1 - P_A - C_B\]
For example, if \(P_A = 0.4\) and \(C_A = 0.1\), then \(W_A = 0.4(1) + 0.6(0) - 0.1 = 0.3\).
Because \(W_A + W_B = 1 - C_A - C_B < 1\), war destroys value. The bargaining range runs from \(P_A - C_A\) to \(P_A + C_B\), and its width is \(C_A + C_B\).
Therefore, each side is incentivized to find a settlement that falls within the bargaining range, as value gained for each side there is greater than any payoff attained through war.

text:
Win Sets and Ratifications
A win set is a set of possible international agreements that can obtain domestic approval. The overlap between the win sets of the negotiating states determines whether a mutually ratifiable bargain exists.
When two countries have large win sets, then it it likely they will be able to come to an agreement, this however, reduces leverage because both parties know that each side has room to concede.
With a small win set, this makes coming to an agreement harder. Likewise a smaller win set means that a country has less incentive to give leeway to the opposing negotiation.

title: Lecture 10-12-2026
text:
Determinants of Win Set Size

Domestic preferences and coalitions: A wide distribution of acceptable outcomes can enlarge the win set. Deep polarization or powerful veto groups have the ability to shrink the size.
Political Institutions: Ratification rules, legilatures, courts, coalition governements, etc. all affect the size of the win set.

Why Leaders Go To War (Cont.)

In-Out-Group Mechanism

Only works when the group is small and has a pre-existing cohesion.
If a society is already highly bipolar then these hypothesus are not likely to hold.

Rally Effects

These effects are small and short lived
E.g. in previous lecture Argentinian president popularity during Falklands War.
In some cases there are exceptions like Winston Churcill during WWII, but that required a massive external threat.
George Bush’s initial victory in Iraq gave him a boost but that boost was so small it did not even help him achieve re-election.
Another criticism of this mechanism is that the public is not naive, they question why leaders go to war, they realize that leaders may initiate wars because they are desperate for popularity.
The positive effects of rallying are smaller just before elections.

Scapegoat mechanism

The ability to blame domestic problems on external threats
It’s hard to associate all domestic issues with external threats.

Gambling of Resurrection

This can be argued to be the worst position a leader can be in. For a leader to want to gamble on starting a war to potentially win re-election is a very desperate mechanism. This mechanism does not in many ways help a leader in terms of gaining electoral victory.
Costly wars can also inflict punishment and further negative outcomes rather than a higher chance of re-election.


Each of these four mechanisms have significant shortcomings and lack significant empirical findings.
Empirical Tests for Diversionary Mechanism
In order to test for this there must be specific domestic patterns: 1. Low Leader Approval 2. Economic Crisis With those issues in place studies look at the correlation between those domestic issues and a state’s propensity to go to war.
Studies have found that there is positive correlation between states experiencing these issues and therefore can said to prove to some degree that there is evidence of diversionary theory.
These problems cannot be said to cause conflict or war, meaning that it is difficult to cause causation between those domestic patterns and the probability of a state to initate/engage in conflict.
Many of these studies have focused on the United States because approval ratings on US presidents are widely available. The US is also one of the only states that can freely initiate conflict without significant costs. This is called major power bias. There was strong evidence with regards to the US in terms of domestic conflicts and positive correlation with external conflict. But when smaller powers like the UK or Israel were studied the same evidence was not found.

Strategic Conflict Avoidance

Targets of conflict tend to avoid conflicts against unpopular leaders because they know they have some incentive to engage in conflict. By this logic other countries should be less likely to go to war against the US during election periods. The enemy would want to avoid the rally affects of attacking a state.
Wars that the US has fought in tend to be initiated early on during a US president’s tenure, not near election periods.
In the US the president enjoys a ‘honeymoon period’ where the presidents approval rating is positive early on during his term. (Usually around the first six months). Most conflicts or war occur during the early period. The enemy specifically does not want to provide any political benefit to the US. This supports the logic of strategic conflict avoidance.
But this means that if you are an unpopular leader and you know the enemy would want to avoid conflict this means you could theoretically levy huge demands. The target therefore would want to avoid conflict but this is where the theory breaks down as to some degree super unreasonable demands could still incentivize the opposing nation to want to engage in conflict.

text:
Democracies are not inherently more peacful towards autocracies.
Democracies tend to be more peaceful towards other democracies. However, democracies are as likely as autocracies to initate interstate conflicts.
Diatic Democratic Peace: Democracies are more peacful to eachother but just as violent as other political systems when not dealing with other democracies.


Democratic norms tend to have less human rights violations, and they tend to be lesser in severity when compared to autocracy. Autocracies are more likely to use violence to resolve domestic disputes.
Key Assumptions*

Externalization:
Institutionalization: Selectorate Theory - The fundamental difference between autocratic and democractic societies is the size of winning coalition. When multiple people have a say in domestic politics are called the selectorate. The support of the selectorate for a leader is not necessary for their political survival, for example you want people to support your party when you exit office so they will elect your party. The same applies to autocracies, in fact it’s more severe there because their literal survival is on the line if they lose power.

In order for leaders to accomplish their survival they must understand whose support is necessary for survival. Support of the entire selectorate tends to not be neccesary, the members whose support is necessary for the survival of the leader is considered the “winning coalition”. For example in an autocracy this “winning coalition” might be just the military leadership, etc.
In a democracy the winning coalition tends to be much larger than that of the winning coalition in an autocracy. In a democractic society the winning coalition tends to be broad public support.
Autocratic leaders tend to use private goods to entice military leadership to support their regime. Private goods are like patronage goods, they are given only to a small group of peoples.
In democratic societies, leaders tend to win broad public support (or support of their winning coalition) via the provision to the general public of public goods. Public goods tend to be more effecient at capturing winning coalition than private goods because it can grab larger support than the scarce private goods.
Assumption War Outcomes are a public good. Meaning a democratic leader must win active wars in order to survive as a leader. Therefore, democratic leaders tend to be very cautious in selecting when to engage in wars, and when they do engage in war they tend to select easier opponents to ensure positive outcomes in wartime. In autocracies, leaders have a lesser incentive to see positive outcomes in wars and therefore autocracies tend to have more wreckless foreign policy.

However this outcome could be argued to be wrong because in a democratic society the outcome of a war tends not to benefit the totality of the winning coalition, instead it behaves more like a private good because it benefits a select few while still imposing costs on the broad public.


Constraints Persepective: Regardless of regime type, many people do not want to pay the huge cost of war. Democratic leaders have to pay more attention to public support/aversion to any given conflict. This plays heavily into their decision to decide to fight a war or not.
Democracies are more transparent than autocracies. Information is more freely available in democracies. Economic data published by China is less trusworthy. War and conflict is more likely when there is large uncertainty. When democracies are in crisis there tends to be less uncertainty, which means less conflict. Democracies have more informational advantages which means they are more certain and therefore much less likely to engage in conflict. When democracies make threats therefore, they tend to be more credible. When democratic leaders make a public announcement or a threat, it is politically costly, this is called audience talk, because the threat ties to democratic leaders hands with his winning coalition, the democratic leaders more likely to follow through because he will pay a much higher political cost. If the democratic leader doesn’t follow through he pays a high audience cost.
Democratic citizens do not want to fight against other democracies. Democratic public opinion has a strong sway on democratic leaders to prevent war against other democracies.
Socialization: If you are brought up in a system where it is not normal to use force or violence against opposition, you will tend not to use, the same could be inversely said about those raised under autocratic systems. This explanations shortcoming is that it points more to a monotonic democratic peace, but this peace lacks empirical evidence.

text:
Types of Aid
Grants are one country or organization giving another money, this money does not have to be repaid.
Loans:

Concessional Loans: Loans who terms are favorable (i.e. a lower interest rate)
Non-Concessional Loans: A loan whose terms are harsher, higher interest rates, shorter payback period. Often times associated with development financing.

Foreign Aid is aimed at helping recipient countries to improve economic conditions and increase growth. Concessional Loans or Grants are usually used here.
Non-conessional loans are considered foreign aid but they are more associated with financing rather than a beneficial foreign aid. This is what seperates US foreign aid from Chinese foreign aid.

Most foreign aid provided by the US is grants, Chinese aid is mostly non-concessional loans.
Humanitarian aid
Military aid, technical aid, personnel assistance, are further types of aid, helping a country pay for their military.
Conditional Aid: A type of aid that requires the recipient country to make some policy concessions. E.g. if you democraticze your electoral system we will provide you aid.
Tied Aid: Another conditional aid type, this is foreign aid that is tied. You can get this aid however, you must purchase the goods for this project that are necessary for this project from companies in my country.
Direct Cash Transfer: Donors or organizaiton provide recipients cash directly as a form of aid.



Reasons Why Aid is Often Ineffective

How do donors strategic incentives undermine aid effectiveness.

Donor countries provide aid not just to help the recipeint country. When the goal is just economic growth aid tends to be more successful. However, when the aid’s goal is to achieve some return/goal in return aid tends to be less effective.
When donors only care about policy concessions from the target they tend to not worry about how the aid is actually spent/used.
This benefits dictators more often than not because dictators are more readily able to provide policy concessions in exchange for aid. The dictator has no reason therefore to actually use the aid to help his economy etc.

Aid can help undermine local industry

Imagine a donor country providing a massive supply of wheat to help with a famine in a country. This is generally good as people get fed because of the aid. However, that recipient countries agricultural industry will likely collapse as the supply of wheat will drop prices and now that are not able to sell their produce at a profit.
Consider also hospital education, local industries will become less competitive with low cost services and products that are provided by donors.
Dutch Disease: A situation where a large influx of foreign captial (unearned income) foreign aid or resource revenue ends up decreasing the competitiveness of local industries that export goods.
This additional capital creates an appreciation in local wages creating a situation where local industries cannot keep up with the increase in wages.
The foreign capital should be exchanged to foreign currency creating a high demand for that currency. That reduction in supply of local currency. That appreciation in local currency creates a higher cost of production for local firms producing goods.

How does foreign aid influence local incentives for economic growth and development

Recipent governments that receieve foreign aid money do not have to necessarily use that aid to encourage economic growth and development.
They can instead use that aid for the benefit of the incumbent regime.
In the case where the recipent country is a dictatorship, the government can use that aid to to survive and strengthen his regime rather than actually helping the local economy.
The private parties that keep the regime in power are typically also benefitted as a result rather than the populace generally of the recipeint dictatorship.
Corrupt economic structure will hinder economic growth. Recipient government has less incentive to go through difficult reforms to fix up corrupt economic conditions, instead they can just continue to receive more money.
If recipient cotunry is more dependent on tax revenue then they are more accountable to their citizens and therefore they are more likely to use aid to benefit their economicy and by proxy their own tax revenue.

A recipient country with a leader who has a long time horizon. Roving bandits are leaders with short time horizons. They want to extract rent as much as possible right now, even if the extraction destroys the economy. They want to extract as much rent as possible in a short time. When they receive foreign aid they just want to extract rents from that foreign aid.
Leaders with long time horizons, they look far ahead into the future. These leaders have an incentive to promote the economic growth of their country and they implement an optimal tax rate. They tend to use aid more efficeiently to promote economic growth of their country.

Donor countries provide aid in exchange for policy concessions. In recipient countries as long as they recieve money they are happy to give what the donor wants. This typically applies to countries with a small selectorate, the policy concession as a result of the exchange of aid. As long as the recipient country gets the concessions it’s looking for, the foreign aid is considered a policy exchange.
Even though the target country cannot promote economic growth using the aid, the donor country is satisified as their goal is the policy concessions.



Sanctions
Instruments of sanctions:
Thes

Comprehensive - Broad restrictions across much of a countries econmoicy (both trade, financial sanctions, travel bans)
Targeted (Smart) sanctions - A narrow scope of sanctions, these attempt to prevent negagtive spill-overs from something like comprehensive sanctions which can hurt the citizenry of a target country. These targeted sanctions try to target specific companies or individuals directly attempting to affect people have more influence with the government.
Primary Sanctions - These involve limiting economic interactions with the sending countries business with the target business of the recipeitn countries. Consider the US ban on chips to China as a primary sanction. The entities that have to comply with sanctions are the senders countries companies.
Seoncdary Sanctions - The imposition of limits on economic trade on the target country.

Depending on the instrument of sanctions:

Import Bans, Shipping Restritciton (Trade restrictions)
Banking cutoff, Debt Limits, Limits on Reserve Access. (Financial Sancitons)
Arms Embargos, Trade Restrictions (Economic Sanctions depending on the instruments).


Target countries will often refuse to comply with demands despite high cost of sanctions.
These economic costs tend to not always translate to political costs. The burden of sanctions tend to be on the citizenry of the recipient country. However, autocratic regimes tend to still be able to provide for their small private selectorate and remain in power.
Target countries can still find ways to generate reveneues while under sanction especially when they trade inelastic goods. Alternative trading routes/partners for goods like oils still enables that country to generate revenue despite the ban from the sending country.
This enables the leader of the recipent coutnry to survive as leader since he can still provide his private selectorte adequate private goods.

If the senders demand is too large (politically) the target country can be willing to bear economic cost since the political demand might be to great.
The target regime may be willing to bear the economic cost since otherwise the political cost is to high inversely.

Sample Selection Bias: Sometimes the threat of sanctions can force a recipient country to comply before the sanctions are actually applied. Since empirical studies cannot account for these situations this creates a survivorship bias in terms of cases where sanctions were successful were not accounted for. The sending country did not need to actualyl apply the sanctions. The inclusion of only cases where sanctions were actually applied creates a sample of less effective situations when sanctions are applied. This underestimates the actual effectiveness of sanctions.
Self Selection Bias: Senders self-select themselves into a subset of successful sanctions. They choose sanctions that are likely to succeed. This introduces a bias that creates a non-random selection and creates a situation where the effectivness of sanctions appear greater than they actually are.

Multilateral Sanctions 
Empirical studies have found multilateral sanctions have agreater effectiveness at getting political outcomes. This requires many countries to act together in imposing sanctions.
However, getting many countries to work together to impose sanctions has a performative issue as there is a collective action problem. Each country has competing incentives an this requires strong coordination.
Why economic sanctions often fail to destabilize target regimes.

This might just change the leader but leave the same ruling elite in power. That ruling elite is what truly makes the autocratic regime live so the changing of leadership does not necessarily ahieve the desired political outcome.

title: Lecture 10-21-2026
text:
When two states have conflicting interests war is not always the preferred or optimal solution. But it still maybe unpopular for a leader domestically to do nothing. Attacking a state militarily is costly and risky therefore economic sanctions maybe instead a preferred method to take action and satisfy domestic yearn for action.
Economic sanctions are considered a coercive foreign policy tool as the goal is to change the other state’s behavior. If the cost of such a policy then the target may reconsider it’s behavior.
Purposes of Economic Sanction:

Deterrance

The goal is to prevent other countries from taking a certain action. The goal of deterrance can only be realized in the future. If a country expects another state to show a certain behavior in the future, then a state might levy sanctions to deter that other country from taking that action. Deterrance can be either direct or indirect. Direct deterrance means a state is protecting it’s own interests from the other states behavior in the future. Indirect deterrance is to protect a protege country, in this case a state might make a threat to protect a nation that is allied to itself.
A popular method of deterrance is a show of force, but in a global economy, economic pressure tends to be more effective.

Compellance

Compellance is not about deterring other states behavior. It is about changing the current behavior of other states. For example, the US might levy sanctions against Iran for their ongoing production of nuclear weapons. Economic sanctions are a popular compellance method as the alternative is military action.


Countries implementing sanctions are called ‘senders’. On the other end, the country that is receiving sanctions is considered the ‘target’.
Trade restrictions, financial restrictions:

Trade

Import bans, export controls, shipping limits, are examples of trade restrictions. The idea is to weaken the other states’ production capacity and access to goods and services. Trade restrictions often create costs across the target economy.

Financial Sanctions

These are becoming more popular as modern ecnomies depend on financial assets, banking systems, and access to currency markets. The sanctions can heavily reduce the targets economic flexibility.

Travel Bans

Banning travel of foreign peoples to a given country can also be a form of sanctions. For example, Russian dignitaries are not allowed to enter certain countires.

Military Sanctions

Military sanctions such as arms embargos, restrictions in military assistance. With an arms embargo a country who might be desperate for weaponry might be targeted with militarty sanctions when other states ban the export of miltiary assets to that country. Additionally, a country who wants to deliver weapons to other countries might be targeted with military sanctions if that country is prevented from exporting weapons.
Restrictions on military assistance can apply to countries whose militaries depend on outside assistance. For example, Pakistan’s military depends on the US for anti terrorism efforts. Reducing or removing militar aid is a form of military sanctions. If a target country is heavily dependant on the sender countries weapon system then they can experience military sanctions when the sender country restsricts assistance/training with those systems.

Most sanctions are implemented by three entities in the world. 60-70% of unilateral economic sanctions were implemented by the United States. Then the UN and European Union also implement many economic sanctions.
If the sender is not economically powerful enough to impose economic sanctions then the sender is likely not willing to implement economic sanctions. A sender’s economy must be strong enough to implement economic sanctions. Economic sanctions implement costs on both the target economy but also on the sender’s economy. For example, the US ban on exports of certain computer chips to China means that China will not benefit from those advanced chips, but likewise US firms that produce these chips will have to accept less revenue since they are effectively cut off from a large market of potential customers.
These economic costs can translate into political cost. If foreign policy is expected to hurt domestic economics then the voting base of the the leader in power may be less likely to support that leader since their economic sanctions are imposing costs on their positions.

Many economic sanctions are designed to undermine the leadership of the target country. For example, the citizens of a target country may not have access to the goods and services they need, likewise, shortages of those goods and services will cause prices in the target country to rise.
If the target country is an importer of inelastic goods then countries will have a tougher time sending sanctions related to those goods.
‘inelastic’ goods are goods that are necessities to all peoples.
In autocratic regimes, those regimes are able to survive the economic costs of sanctions even though the public may have a negative view of the leaderships’ behavior that led to sanctions. Autocratic regimes are likely to participate in black market activity.
Democratic leaders are more accountable for economic costs and are more likely to experience higher political costs from economic sanctions.
Economic sanctions do not substantially increase the failure of leadership in autocratic regimes. In some cases they actually increase the odds of an autocratic leaders survival in office. Citizens in autocratic countries tend to blame sender countries more than their own leadership. This perspective of foreign opression can create a rally effect around that autocratic leader.

Sanction Busters are countries who interfere in the process of economic sanctions implemented by senders. For example, Iranian oil is not suppsoed to be imported by other countries in the world. However, certain countries are strategically purchasing Iranian oil to intentially ‘bust’ American sanctions there.
Targeted smart sanctions are more effective than general sanctions. These targeted sanctions can reduce negative spill-overs, these sanctions do not effect the citizens of the targeted country. Instead they target individuals in the target country.
